mcqs.question: A grammar for arithmetic expressions parses "1 + 2 * 3" in two different valid ways, giving 9 in one parse and 7 in the other. What does this indicate about the grammar?
options: The grammar has a typo in its terminal symbols
The grammar is ambiguous — the string has more than one valid parse tree
This is expected and harmless as long as the language compiles
mcqs.explanation: A grammar producing two distinct valid parse trees for the same string is, by definition, ambiguous — and that's exactly the practical problem here, since the two trees give genuinely different meanings (9 vs 7). This has nothing to do with whether the grammar is context-free (it can be both context-free and ambiguous), and it is not harmless — it makes program meaning undefined until resolved.

mcqs.question: A language is known to be context-free. What does the Chomsky hierarchy guarantee about whether it's also a regular language?
options: It's automatically regular too, since context-free is a subset of regular
It must be context-sensitive but never regular
Being context-free tells you nothing about its relationship to regular languages
It's not necessarily regular — context-free is a strictly larger class that contains all regular languages plus more
mcqs.explanation: The hierarchy nests regular ⊂ context-free, meaning every regular language is also context-free, but not every context-free language is regular (e.g. balanced parentheses is context-free but not regular). So being context-free is a weaker guarantee than being regular, not a stronger one — you can't conclude regularity just from context-freeness.

mcqs.question: Why can't a pushdown automaton recognize the language {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, even though it can recognize {aⁿbⁿ}?
options: A single stack can match one count against another (push on a's, pop on b's) but has no way to simultaneously check a third independent count against the same stack
PDAs can only process strings of even length
The alphabet {a,b,c} has too many distinct symbols for a PDA to handle
PDAs cannot process any string longer than a fixed constant length
mcqs.explanation: A PDA's single stack is enough to verify two counts match (push while reading a's, pop while reading b's, check for an empty stack) but once the a's are consumed and the stack is empty, there's no remaining mechanism to also verify the c count matches — that requires tracking two independent counts at once, beyond what one stack supports. This has nothing to do with string length or alphabet size.

mcqs.question: Using the grammar S -> ( S ) S | ε, why does no derivation ever produce the string ")("?
options: Because the grammar only allows strings of even length
Because every production that introduces a ')' immediately follows an already-placed matching '(' from that same rule application — there's no rule that can generate a ')' as the very first symbol
Because ')(' contains two distinct symbols, and this grammar only supports one symbol per string
Because the grammar is ambiguous, and ambiguous grammars can't generate any strings
mcqs.explanation: Every application of the S -> ( S ) S rule places an open paren before its own inner S expansion and its matching close paren after — so a close paren can only ever appear once a corresponding open paren has already been placed earlier in the derivation, making a leading ')' unreachable. Even-length is true of valid strings here but isn't the reason ')(' specifically fails, and ambiguity (this grammar isn't ambiguous) is unrelated to whether a string is generable at all.
